cards.headline: Dozens killed in strikes on Yemeni village blamed on Saudi Arabia

pages.text: Large crowds gathered in Sanaa, Yemen, to mourn dozens of people killed in strikes on the village of al-Shariya, located outside the capital. The Houthis, an Iran-backed group that controls the capital, stated that a Saudi Arabian strike on November 7, 2026, killed 44 people, including 21 children, and injured 40 others. The group's Almasirah television reported an additional strike occurred as emergency personnel attempted to dig out survivors, though AFP could not verify that claim. During the funeral procession, mourners prayed at the Mosque of the People—formerly the Saleh Mosque before being renamed by the Houthis—and chanted slogans against America and Israel. Resident and farmer Daifallah Sarhan told AFP that the victims were innocent people having meals with their families when the strikes hit.

The casualties in al-Shariya are part of a resumption in fighting that began over the summer. According to the UN, this conflict has killed more than 1,600 people and displaced more than 300,000 people in Yemen. In a separate development, G7 foreign ministers met in Paris on November 9 and 10, issuing a joint statement that condemned continued Houthi strikes inside Yemen and against Saudi Arabia. The ministers, representing Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK, the US, and the EU, stated that these attacks included strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure. The G7 urged Iran to stop arming and supporting the Houthi group and called for the group to immediately cease all military action to allow an inclusive political process to resume.

cards.headline: More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food insecurity, UN warns

pages.text: More than one million people in Lebanon face acute food insecurity, according to a warning from the United Nations. A joint statement by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme, and the Lebanese agriculture ministry reported that nearly a quarter of the population faces crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse. The UN bodies called for “urgent action” to address the situation, noting that the number of people affected is expected to rise to 1.15 million by the middle of the year. The UN defines these levels of food insecurity as households facing malnutrition or being only able to meet minimum needs through emergency measures, such as selling assets.

The food crisis follows years of war and an unprecedented economic collapse that began in 2019. The UN stated that employment opportunities remain limited, savings have been depleted, and debt remains high, while the rising cost of food, fuel, and other essentials continues to strain household budgets. The UN expressed particular concern regarding conditions in conflict-affected areas of south Lebanon, as well as in impoverished regions in the north and east of the country.

Lebanon has endured two successive wars with neighboring Israel since 2023. Lebanese authorities estimate the cost of the two wars between Israel and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah since October 2023 is approximately $27 billion. The last war, launched in March in support of Hezbollah’s patron Iran, displaced more than one million people in Lebanon; that number fell to around 300,000 after violence subsided in June.

cards.headline: Ebola outbreak in Democratic Republic of the Congo exceeds 11,000 cases

pages.text: The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has surpassed 11,000 cases, according to Congolese government data. The Bundibugyo virus, which has no known vaccine or treatment, has infected 11,042 people and killed 5,387, according to the health ministry. This represents nearly half of those infected and marks the country's deadliest outbreak. The virus has spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces and has also reached Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria. While the World Health Organization (WHO) reports that almost 3,000 people have recovered and transmission is slowing in some areas, the outbreak remains a public health emergency of international concern. The current situation has already resulted in at least three times the number of cases and deaths in the time since it was declared in mid-May compared to the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak, which saw 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.

Authorities are struggling to contain the disease due to armed conflicts, a health system crisis, poor roads, and rainy weather. Insecurity has become a major obstacle to the response. During an attack on the town of Cantine-Aloya, 66 civilians were killed, including three health workers, and three health facilities were looted and burned. In Tshopo province, a nurse was killed and another health worker was badly injured during an attack while responding to an Ebola alert. Other incidents include a grenade found near a health zone office and stones thrown at a vehicle conducting safe and dignified burials. These attacks, along with violence fueled by mistrust and misinformation, have targeted medical professionals and facilities. Health authorities are calling for a halt to fighting in the Ituri and North Kivu provinces to allow unhindered access to the sick. Additionally, more than 1,000 contacts have been lost to follow up, and three confirmed cases are unaccounted for.

cards.headline: Former Iraqi lawmaker Ahmed al-Alwani found dead in Beirut apartment

pages.text: Lebanese authorities are investigating the death of former Iraqi lawmaker Ahmed Suleiman Al-Alwani, who was found dead in an apartment in the Tariq al-Jdideh neighborhood of Beirut on November 10, 2026. Lebanese security and judicial investigators are looking into whether Al-Alwani was deliberately lured to the city and if political motives were behind the killing. Preliminary findings from a Lebanese judicial source indicate the 57-year-old was strangled and had been struck on the head. Al-Alwani’s office described the death as a “premeditated assassination” and a “treacherous crime,” calling for a transparent investigation to identify those who planned and carried out the act. Lebanon’s top prosecutor, Judge Ahmed Rami al-Hajj, is personally overseeing the investigation, which is being conducted by the Information Branch of Lebanon’s Internal Security Forces.

Investigators are focusing on individuals who reportedly met Al-Alwani at Beirut’s Rafic Hariri International Airport following his arrival on November 5 and accompanied him to an apartment in the Afif Al-Tibi area of Tariq Al-Jadideh. A Lebanese national suspected of involvement has been arrested, and authorities are searching for two Syrian suspects who remain at large. A judicial source told Arab News that investigators are not ruling out the possibility that the perpetrators were Iraqi nationals rather than Syrian. While initial, unconfirmed reports suggested three individuals were suspected of involvement, subsequent information indicated two people were under suspicion, while a third was believed to have been a taxi driver. Lebanese security agencies are reviewing surveillance footage and questioning individuals who were in contact with Al-Alwani to track his movements from his arrival until his body was discovered.

The body was discovered after a real estate agent, attempting to contact Al-Alwani to request an additional payment and extend a two-day, $200 rental agreement, noticed a foul odor coming from the 12th-floor apartment. The agent found the body inside the bathroom, and it was initially transferred to a hospital morgue. The Iraqi Embassy later informed Lebanese security agencies that Al-Alwani had been reported missing, which helped investigators identify the deceased. According to preliminary information, Al-Alwani’s family had received no ransom demands or requests for money following his disappearance. Iraq’s Ambassador to Lebanon, Mohammed Reda Al-Husseini, stated the embassy is working to expedite DNA testing to facilitate the repatriation of Al-Alwani’s body to Baghdad while following the ongoing security investigations.

cards.headline: Israeli forces launch incursions into Syria's Quneitra Governorate and set farmland ablaze

pages.text: Israeli forces carried out fresh incursions into Syria's Quneitra Governorate, expelling olive harvesters from southern farmland and sparking a fire on agricultural land in the north, according to Syrian state television. Alikhbaria TV reported that an Israeli patrol advanced into an area west of the town of al-Rafid in southern Quneitra, where troops searched olive harvesters before expelling them from their fields and preventing them from continuing their work. In northern Quneitra, Israeli forces fired smoke grenades at farmland near the village of Taranja, igniting a fire; the broadcaster did not specify the extent of the damage. On November 10, 2026, Israeli forces established a checkpoint at the entrance to the town of Jaba al-Khashab in northern Quneitra to search passersby, the broadcaster said.

cards.headline: Japan Supreme Court rules July 2025 Upper House election held in unconstitutional state

pages.text: The Supreme Court of Japan ruled that the July 2025 Upper House election was conducted in an “unconstitutional state” because vote-value disparities reached up to 3.13. Despite this finding, the court dismissed requests to invalidate the election results. The ruling was issued by the court's Grand Bench, which presided over 16 lawsuits filed by two groups of lawyers across the country seeking to invalidate the election.

Chief Justice Yukihiko Imasaki, who presided over the Grand Bench, stated that the maximum disparity in the election was at a level that raises constitutional concerns. The decision was supported by 10 of the 15 justices, while the remaining five justices found the 2025 election to be constitutional.

cards.headline: DR Congo President Felix Tshisekedi enacts law easing rules for constitutional referendum

pages.text: DR Congo President Felix Tshisekedi has enacted a law that eases the rules for holding a referendum on constitutional matters. The law was enacted via an order read on national television overnight. The opposition has condemned the move, alleging it is an attempt by the 63-year-old president to cling to power by potentially changing the constitution to allow him to run for a third term. Under the current constitution, Tshisekedi, who has been in power since 2019, is required to step down at the end of his second five-year term at the end of 2028.

In an early May news conference, Tshisekedi stated he had not sought a third term but said, “If people want me to have a third term, I will accept.” Opposition parties have recently joined forces to oppose attempts to change the constitution. This opposition group, which recently formed a platform called C64, has struggled to rally large numbers of people in the streets following Tshisekedi's landslide victory in the 2023 election. Demonstrations protesting what the opposition called a “constitutional coup” occurred in Kinshasa and other cities in June and September. Meanwhile, much of the eastern part of the country remains affected by conflict, where the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group has seized swathes of territory.

cards.headline: Thousands in Gaza face lethal conditions as 150,000 shelters await Israeli approval

pages.text: Tens of thousands of Palestinians in Gaza have been left in waterlogged and damaged tents following deadly storms at the weekend, according to aid agencies. While 150,000 new shelters are being held outside Gaza, they are currently awaiting Israeli approval to enter the territory. The United Nations reports that 940,000 people in Gaza are living in makeshift tents in areas at risk of flooding without protection from heavy rainfall. The threat of flooding has increased because facilities for pumping out storm water are not operating due to a lack of power.

At least four Palestinian children and a woman were killed as heavy rains and wind battered fragile, leaky tents. Aid workers warn that disease could spread rapidly unless families receive new shelters and ways to stay warm. Sanitation infrastructure has been destroyed, resulting in sewage spewing into people's tents. Raed Jamal, a displaced Palestinian, reported that his children are sick and his clothes were soaked, noting that he had to use pots to collect rainwater falling through holes in his tent's roof. Jamal shared videos with the Guardian showing his tent shaking in the wind.

Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP), a UK-based charity, expressed concern regarding a rise in health problems as families live in flooded tents with no alternative shelter. Mai Elawawda, a communications officer for MAP in Gaza, stated that medical teams expect to see more respiratory illnesses and other health complications linked to cold, damp, and overcrowded conditions. Elawawda added that there are fears more children could die from hypothermia, similar to what occurred last winter.

cards.headline: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid reported surge in Russian recruitment

pages.text: Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, following reports of a spike in recruitment by Russia from the Southeast Asian nation. According to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project, a 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to participate in a Russian assault. The man reached Ukrainian-held territory after his group came under drone attack and was subsequently captured by Ukrainian forces. The I Want to Live project reported that approximately 283 Indonesians were recruited to fight for Russia against Ukraine in the first nine months of the year, compared to no more than 10 recruited in the previous three years.

The Indonesian government has urged Moscow to ensure no Indonesians are drafted into its military. Indonesian foreign ministry spokesperson Yvonne Mewengkang stated that the government asked the Russian government to take all necessary steps to ensure no Indonesians are recruited into the Russian military or any other military-related position in Russia through any avenues. Mewengkang added that Indonesia is particularly concerned about recruitment practices that could constitute human trafficking. This follows the reported death in October of an Indonesian national serving with the military. Days after that statement, Indonesian police said they had identified a human trafficking syndicate targeting Indonesian nationals using social media and messaging apps to recruit victims.

The Russian embassy in Jakarta did not immediately respond to questions regarding the alleged recruitment effort. This development follows reports of Russia seeking foreign mercenaries to sustain its war in Ukraine, which began in February 2022. In February, Kenya’s intelligence services reported that more than 1,000 Kenyans had been lured to fight for Russia. A growing number of people from various African countries, including Kenya, Uganda, and South Africa, have also been reported as being lured to the frontline.

cards.headline: Salvadoran military helicopters strike gang leader's home in Haiti

pages.text: Salvadoran military helicopters launched rocket strikes against a home in the Haitian countryside that President Nayib Bukele identified as the headquarters of a powerful gang leader. On November 10, 2026, Bukele released video footage showing the strikes, which sent plumes of smoke into the air and caused men to flee the targeted buildings. Bukele stated the attack destroyed a home belonging to Wilson Joseph, the leader of the 400 Mawozo group, who is also known as Lanmò San Jou. Joseph was not killed in the attack.

The offensive followed an interaction on the social platform X, where Bukele had asked for the location of Joseph's house days earlier. Several accounts responded to the request with what appeared to be precise coordinates. Following the strikes, Bukele wrote, “We kept our promise.” Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé responded to the video on X, stating he “salutes the commitment of the Salvadoran forces in the fight against gangs” and telling Bukele, “Hats off to President Nayib Bukele, for your support and commitment to the national fight against gangs.” Additionally, on November 10, 2026, the Dominican Republic, which shares the island of Hispaniola with Haiti, said it was working with El Salvador in the fight against gangs.

cards.headline: US House Republicans block impeachment effort against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth

pages.text: On November 10, 2026, the US House of Representatives voted 211 to 204 to refer impeachment articles against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee. The vote effectively blocked an impeachment bid introduced by Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who had warned that referring the resolution to a committee would kill the initiative because of the limited time remaining in the current Congress. Massie, an outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, was the only Republican to oppose the procedural move to refer the matter to the committee. Following the vote, Massie compared his Republican colleagues in the outgoing Congress to passengers on the Titanic, stating, “They know it's a sinking ship but committed to stay on board.”

The impeachment resolution brought eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth. Massie accused the Defense Secretary of waging war on Iran without congressional authorization and of abuse of power. The articles also included allegations regarding strikes against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie described as “extrajudicial killings,” as well as the 2025 conflict with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. Additionally, Massie accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech after an attempt to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video in which Kelly urged military and intelligence personnel to stand up against illegal orders. During a Pentagon press conference on November 10, 2026, Hegseth dismissed the accusations as “slander,” “sabotage,” a “farce,” and a “stunt.”

President Trump celebrated the outcome on Truth Social, stating the effort “has miserably FAILED” and describing Hegseth as a “Great American Patriot” who had been “exonerated.” Vice President JD Vance also commented that Hegseth had “obviously not” committed impeachable offenses. While the current Republican majority in the House prevented the impeachment from reaching a full vote, Democrats are expected to take control of both chambers of Congress in January. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries stated, “This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning.” Additionally, the White House's top lawyer, Will Scharf, sent a letter to incoming House oversight committee chair Robert Garcia, threatening Democrats with criminal investigations if they launch oversight inquiries that are “deployed to harass and aggrandize” administration members or verge into “blatant criminality.”

cards.headline: Millions participate in Spain's first general strike in 14 years to protest rising housing costs

pages.text: Millions of people across Spain joined a nationwide 24-hour general strike to protest a deepening housing crisis. The stoppage, which was called for by tenants' associations and later backed by workers' unions, saw approximately four million people take part by midday, according to the Confederation of Tenants’ Association. This marks the first general strike in the country in 14 years and occurs weeks before a snap election scheduled for November 29, in which the far right could potentially gain power. The housing crisis has become a central political debate, following the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid. According to estimates from the central bank, Spain has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, a figure set to grow to more than a million by 2028. As fewer families can afford to buy, the number of renters has risen sharply; Spain's youth council reports the average rent is €1,176 ($1,315), which is equivalent to 99% of the average young person's salary.

Participation in the strike was reported as high across several sectors, including 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection, though unions noted participation was uneven across the country. The strongest support was reported in coastal regions such as Catalonia and Andalusia, where housing costs have been particularly acute. In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks, some using burning tyres, as public transport came to a near-standstill and key roads, including the AP-7 motorway, were blocked in both directions. In Madrid, thousands of demonstrators entered the city's main boulevard, temporarily halting traffic, and scuffles occurred between picketers and police near the country's main wholesale market. Strikers at the Mercamadrid wholesale market reported that police used pepper spray on the crowd, prompting at least 13 people to seek medical attention. Additionally, some airlines reported disruptions to flights in and out of Spain due to participation by airport and airline workers.

The strike follows political friction regarding housing legislation. The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass laws to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties. While Sanchez's government approved two extraordinary decrees introducing measures similar to the rejected housing reforms, Sanchez called the early November 29 election in hopes of shoring up support. The government stated the strike is being held “in favor of rights” rather than against anyone, though sources close to Sanchez's inner circle have suggested it is “against the opposition.” In Madrid, the labor action added to an ongoing strike by teachers that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions. The general strike also follows a strike by rail workers the previous day regarding two major deadly train crashes.

cards.headline: Brazil's top electoral court fines Meta 7.5 million reais for failing to comply with judicial orders

pages.text: Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) unanimously ruled on November 10, 2026, to fine Meta 7.5 million reais ($1.34 million; €1.22 million) for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during the country's presidential election. The court stated that the US tech giant, which owns Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, missed deadlines and lacked transparency in its investigation. While the fine was imposed, the judicial body has so far found no evidence that Meta deliberately acted to influence the election outcome. Reporting judge Marco Aurelio Belizze wrote in his ruling that there was no preliminary evidence indicating intentional actions were taken to influence the election, noting that such a conclusion would require robust evidence produced through appropriate legal proceedings.

The ruling follows a complaint filed by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's coalition ahead of the October 25 runoff vote. The coalition accused Meta of “algorithmic manipulation” that favored his far-right rival, Flavio Bolsonaro. Meta told the court it had implemented measures to guarantee equal treatment for both campaigns and stated it will defend itself against what it called “false allegations.”

cards.headline: Russia and Ukraine agree to a large exchange of prisoners of war

pages.text: Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, according to officials participating in U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates. Vladimir Medinsky, head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led the Ukrainian delegation, confirmed the planned exchange following two days of negotiations. While Russia and Ukraine have swapped prisoners periodically during their nearly five-year war, this agreement follows the first meeting between the delegations in nine months.

Following the conclusion of the talks in Abu Dhabi, Jared Kushner, son-in-law of President Donald Trump, stated that he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on November 12, 2026, to meet with President Vladimir Putin. They are scheduled to fly to Dublin after the Moscow meeting to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

U.S. officials said they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts, which have so far failed to deliver significant results. The context of these negotiations has changed since the last meeting between the delegations took place in February in Geneva. The Trump administration faces a changing political landscape as Democrats, who could take over Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections, may demand more support for Ukraine.

cards.headline: Iranian security chief threatens to strike US bases in Europe if used for attacks

pages.text: Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei has threatened to strike United States military bases in Europe and other distant regions if they are used to launch attacks against Iran. Speaking in an interview with Lebanon-based Al Mayadeen TV, Rezaei stated that Iran would target American military installations, including those it has not previously attacked, if American aircraft take off from such bases to bomb the Islamic republic. He added that Iran may even strike certain islands that are assumed to be beyond the reach of Iranian missiles.

The threats come amid an ongoing Middle East war that began on February 28, following US-Israeli strikes that killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. In response to those strikes, Iran launched missiles and drones across the region, while militant groups supported by Iran in Lebanon, Yemen, and Iraq also entered the conflict. Tehran has sought to negotiate an end to the war through diplomatic efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan, insisting that Washington unfreeze assets and lift sanctions in exchange for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy conduit that Iran has blockaded since the conflict began.

On November 10, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated there was no need to attack Iran again, citing efforts to undermine its economy. Meanwhile, federal prosecutors in New York unsealed an indictment on November 10, 2026, charging three men with terrorism offenses related to an alleged Iran-backed campaign of nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States. The indictment alleges Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and Mohammed Ali Al-Hassani acted on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi militia Kata'ib Hezbollah—both of which are designated by the US as foreign terrorist organizations—to target Jewish communities and a British air base hosting American troops.

cards.headline: Rights group raises concerns about health of jailed Gaza hospital director

pages.text: Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) has accused Israeli authorities of ignoring the deteriorating health of Dr. Hussam Abu Safia, the jailed director of Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital. The rights group reported that Abu Safia, who was captured by the Israeli army in December 2024 during a raid on the hospital in northern Gaza, is being denied a basic right to an independent medical examination. PHRI stated that the Israel Prison Service has refused to release Abu Safia’s latest medical file. Naji Abbas of PHRI said the doctor has been deprived of his freedom without trial and is being denied an independent medical review.

An independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records, conducted by reviewer Amit Tirosh, showed a weight loss of 14kg (31lb) in four months, a significant drop in haemoglobin levels, and chest pain that was not properly investigated. Tirosh was not permitted to examine Abu Safia in person. Tirosh disputed a finding by an Israeli court that high blood pressure was Abu Safia's only medical problem, stating the ruling “does not line up with the data.”

The concerns regarding Abu Safia follow the rejection of petitions by two Israeli courts. One petition sought to allow Abu Safia to receive an independent medical examination, while another sought the release of 14 doctors from Gaza who are being held in Israeli prisons without charge. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition for the 14 doctors—which included hospital directors and specialists in essential medical fields—finding no grounds to intervene in the Chief of Staff’s decision not to release them. PHRI argued that these prolonged arbitrary detentions, which in some cases have lasted more than two years, violate individual rights and undermine Gaza’s healthcare system by contributing to a severe shortage of medical professionals.

cards.headline: Two U.S. companies apply for deep-sea mining exploration licenses in South Pacific international waters

pages.text: Two U.S. companies have applied to the U.S. government for seabed mining exploration licenses in two large patches of international waters near the Cook Islands, Kiribati, and French Polynesia in the South Pacific Ocean. The applications seek to explore the seabed for mining potential with the eventual goal of extracting and selling minerals. The targeted areas include a 101,064-square-kilometer (39,021-square-mile) pocket of international waters bounded by the exclusive economic zones of the Cook Islands, Kiribati, and French Polynesia, as well as an 89,645-km2 (34,612-mi2) area south of the Cook Islands’ exclusive economic zone. The applicants are Delaware-incorporated American Deep Sea Minerals, Inc. (ADSM) and Florida-based American Ocean Minerals Corporation (AOM).

The applications are part of a broader effort by U.S. companies to stake claims to the international seabed through a U.S. permitting process. This process bypasses the U.N.-linked multilateral body responsible for regulating deep-sea mining on the high seas and protecting the marine environment. Beyond the South Pacific sites, a Mongabay investigation showed that U.S. companies are also seeking rights through this process for large seabed blocks in international waters near Guam in the western Pacific and in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ), a vast area located between Hawai‘i and Mexico. These areas often contain polymetallic nodules, which are avocado-sized rocks containing minerals such as nickel, manganese, copper, and cobalt.

Local government officials and environmental organizations are pushing back against the applications. Louisa Castledine, a spokesperson for the Cook Islands-based ocean advocacy collective Ocean Ancestors, told Mongabay that the plans create a “dangerous pathway of opening up the Pacific region to increased exploitation and vulnerability.” Castledine stated that the companies are testing “every kind of trajectory and angle and strategy and opportunity they can make to extract.”

cards.headline: Iran denies US negotiations and says Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until seven conditions are met

pages.text: Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei dismissed claims of upcoming negotiations with the United States, stating that Tehran is waiting for a response to seven conditions for peace talks. On November 10, 2026, Rezaei told Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen TV that rumors regarding continuing negotiations or holding a meeting in Qatar are a “pure lie.” He alleged that Washington is discussing negotiations to ease economic pressure and reduce oil prices. Rezaei stated that the Strait of Hormuz, a global maritime corridor that Iran has closed, will not reopen until the United States meets Tehran's seven conditions. He described the initial response from the United States as “insufficient and deceptive,” adding that Iran is still waiting for an explicit and clear response.

While Iran has not released the full list of its seven conditions, Rezaei and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi have indicated the demands include lifting sanctions and the US naval blockade, as well as ending fighting on all fronts, specifically Israel’s attacks on Lebanon. Speaking to the state news agency IRNA on November 10, 2026, Araghchi said the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within two days if the demands are met. Araghchi also stated that the conflict with Iran will not be resolved through intensifying sanctions or military means. These statements follow reports from the IRGC that at least three ships had hit mines and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz.

The denial of talks comes as US President Donald Trump expressed seeing “positive momentum” toward ending the conflict between the US, Israel, and Iran. On November 9, 2026, Trump held talks at the White House with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, noting that new attacks on Iran were unnecessary. Qatar serves as a key mediator in the conflict. Despite the reported momentum, the Iranian leadership maintains that no meetings are currently scheduled and that the maritime closure remains tied to the fulfillment of their specific demands.

cards.headline: EU weighs upgrading ties with Syria to counter Russian influence

pages.text: The European Union is considering a broad upgrade in its relationship with Syria, including security sector reform, investment, and the revival of a long-frozen trade accord. According to an EU document seen by Reuters, the bloc aims to draw Damascus closer to Europe and counter the lingering influence of Russia following the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad. The discussion paper was prepared by the EU's diplomatic service ahead of a November 16 meeting of EU foreign ministers. It represents one of the bloc's most ambitious efforts to normalize ties with Syria less than two years after the fall of the Assad regime ended decades of authoritarian rule.

The EU's diplomatic service noted that while Syria's transition is moving forward, challenges remain high. The bloc stated that accelerated progress is needed regarding economic recovery, national reconciliation, and the reintegration of refugees and internally displaced people. To support security-sector reform, the EU is considering trilateral cooperation with Jordan to train Syrian police recruits. These efforts are intended to limit the influence of Russia and other foreign actors in Syria, according to the discussion paper. While the document noted that Moscow's influence has diminished since the post-Assad transition, its continued economic leverage and military presence remain a concern.

Russia previously intervened in Syria's civil war to support the Assad government and secure strategic Mediterranean assets, including the Hmeimim air base and the Tartous naval facility. Since the overthrow, the Kremlin has attempted to secure a new deal with current Syrian authorities to maintain access to these sites. To deepen ties, the EU is proposing to revive an association agreement that was initialled in 2008 but never concluded. This agreement would provide a framework for political dialogue, free trade, and broader cooperation. EU diplomats intend to seek a fresh mandate from EU member countries to negotiate revisions to the pact, using the existing text as a basis for deepening relations.

cards.headline: Canada Post issues stamp honoring Chinese Canadians who performed covert World War II operations

pages.text: Canada Post has issued a new Remembrance Day stamp to honor approximately 150 Chinese Canadians who volunteered for dangerous covert operations during World War II. Although these individuals were barred from serving in the Canadian military at the start of the war, they volunteered for secret missions in 1944 when called upon. The stamp was unveiled in Vancouver on Nov. 3, and a ceremony was held in Toronto on Nov. 10, 2026, alongside the Chinese Cultural Centre of Greater Toronto. The design features a historic black-and-white photograph of Force 136 members awaiting repatriation in 1945, overlaid with the red phoenix insignia of Force 136, with the group's name appearing in English, French, and traditional Chinese.

The honored group consisted of Chinese Canadians recruited for their language skills and their ability to blend in while conducting secret missions behind enemy lines in Japanese-occupied Asia. These volunteers served either with Force 136—a unit of Britain’s Special Operations Executive—or with Australia’s Services Reconnaissance Department. To prepare for these roles, they underwent specialized training in espionage, sabotage, guerrilla warfare, parachuting, and intelligence gathering. Historians noted that the service of Force 136 members helped advance the Allied war effort and contributed to the push for equality within Canada.

At the time of their service, Chinese Canadians faced discrimination and were considered second-class citizens denied basic rights. Many volunteers viewed enlistment as a way to demonstrate commitment to Canada and influence how immigrants were treated. Following the war, the Chinese Exclusion Act was repealed two years later, allowing Chinese Canadians to gain full citizenship rights, including the right to vote. Sharifa Khan of the Chinese Cultural Centre of Greater Toronto stated that the recognition by Canada Post is important for telling these stories to future generations of all Canadians.

cards.headline: Lost 1943 Christmas care package for Canadian soldier discovered in England

pages.text: A Christmas care package intended for a Canadian soldier during the Second World War has been discovered 83 years after it was sent. The package was addressed to Lance-Cpl. Ross Hutton and appears to have been sent by his Aunt Ethel. The discovered package remains largely intact, with the linen bag showing no yellowing. It still contains its original customs form and various items, including cigarettes, bouillon cubes, tea bags, cans of baked beans, tomato juice, cake, meat, socks, and gum.

cards.headline: Toronto police identify man found dead on church lawn in 1992 using genetic genealogy

pages.text: Toronto police have identified a man found dead on a downtown Toronto church lawn more than three decades ago through investigative genetic genealogy. The Toronto Police Service (TPS) confirmed the man, identified as Derek, was a British-born individual who moved to Toronto in the 1970s. He was discovered unresponsive near Queen Street East and Church Street on Sept. 15, 1992. Although police, firefighters, and paramedics attempted life-saving efforts, he was pronounced dead at the scene. Investigators determined at the time that the death was not suspicious. The case remained unsolved for more than 30 years because the man had no identification and traditional investigative methods failed to establish his identity. According to police, Derek was not reported missing until December 1993, approximately 15 months after his body was discovered, following a report filed by his lawyer. No connection was made at that time between the missing-person investigation and the unidentified man found in 1992.

cards.headline: Indigenous stewards in British Columbia advocate for controlled burns to combat wildfires

pages.text: Indigenous stewards in British Columbia are advocating for the use of controlled burns, referred to by Leona Antoine as “good fire,” to manage forests and mitigate wildfire risks. Antoine, a Syilx and Nlaka'pamux former forest firefighter and forestry consultant living in Merritt, B.C., describes how low, patchy fires can clear away dead brush and recycle nutrients back into the soil. This process allows sunlight to reach the ground, which can lead to the growth of fresh green grass, huckleberries, and other traditional medicines within weeks. Antoine's family land in the Nicola River valley is located in British Columbia's increasingly flammable southern Interior, an area near towns such as Lytton and Summerland that have become associated with recent megafires.

The practice of cultural burning was largely outlawed from Indigenous communities during the era when Antoine's grandfather came of age. Proponents suggest that decades of aggressive forest fire suppression, combined with extreme weather fueled by climate change, have left Canadian forests primed to burn. Antoine notes that her practice of using controlled fire is a method she learned from her grandfather to manage the land.

cards.headline: Soldiers from CFB Wainwright fire participate in Remembrance Day ceremonies in Alberta

pages.text: Approximately 300 members of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry (3 PPCLI) are expected to march in a Remembrance Day ceremony in St. Albert, Alberta, on November 11, 2026. This marks the regiment's first public appearance since an October 17 fire at Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright killed four soldiers and injured 39 others. Members of the battalion were among the first responders who helped transport injured soldiers to ambulances and helicopters during the blaze. Two Griffon helicopters, the same type used to evacuate the wounded from Wainwright, will fly over the ceremony just before the moment of silence. Several thousand spectators, including family members of the soldiers, are expected to attend the event.

The October 17 fire occurred during an attack training exercise involving roughly 84 soldiers from the Charlie Company unit of the 3 PPCLI. According to the military, a strong wind sent flames from a grass fire racing onto the troops. The victims killed in the blaze were Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton. Prime Minister Mark Carney described the event as one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are currently looking into the cause and circumstances of the fire.

In Wainwright, Alberta, the annual Remembrance Day service is expected to be the most solemn in recent history, according to Mayor Bruce Pugh. Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is set to attend the Wainwright ceremony alongside other dignitaries, military members, and veterans. Following the fire, Poilievre visited Wainwright to meet injured soldiers, noting the bravery of those who entered fire to rescue others. Military chaplain Lt.-Cmdr. Matthew Squires told CBC that supporting grieving families and visiting injured soldiers in the hospital has been a heavy and challenging experience.

cards.headline: Paramedic widow describes reviving fallen officer before realizing husband was also shot

pages.text: Ashley Ryan, a paramedic of approximately 13 years, told a court in Edmonton, Canada, that she was attempting to revive a fallen officer at the Royal Alexandra Hospital when she realized her husband had also been shot. Ryan provided this account during a victim impact statement read at the sentencing hearing for 22-year-old Dennis Okeymow. Ryan, who was 15 weeks pregnant at the time of the incident, described the moment an ambulance arrived with her husband, Brett Ryan, following the ambush of two officers responding to a domestic disturbance call in March 2023.

The shooting occurred when Brett Ryan and his partner, Constable Travis Jordan, arrived at an apartment building and were ambushed and shot by 16-year-old Roman Shewchuk. Shewchuk, who had a history of mental illness, then turned the gun on himself. Court proceedings revealed that Okeymow had sold the semi-automatic rifle used in the shooting to the teenager weeks earlier. In May, Okeymow was found guilty on 10 charges, including three counts of manslaughter and three counts of criminal negligence causing the deaths of the two officers and the shooter.

In her statement, Ryan recounted cleaning blood and brain matter from her husband's face and beard so that family and friends would not have to witness the condition in which he died. She described the experience of realizing her husband was on the stretcher as a moment of blood-curdling screams that she said will always echo in the ambulance bay.

cards.headline: 17-year-old boy arrested in connection with murder of Ghanaian teenager in the Bronx

pages.text: A 17-year-old boy has reportedly been arrested in connection with the murder of 15-year-old Javits Badu Nkansah Frimpong, a Ghanaian teenager who was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx, New York. The New York Daily News reported the arrest on its Facebook page, marking a development in the investigation into the killing. Details regarding the suspect's identity, the specific charges, and the circumstances of the arrest have not yet been independently established. Javits was fatally shot on the morning of Thursday, October 29, 2026, near East 171st Street and Crotona Place in the Claremont section of the Bronx. He was traveling to DreamYard Preparatory School when he sustained a gunshot wound to the abdomen. Police stated the teenager was shot shortly before 9:30 a.m. and was taken to St. Barnabas Hospital, where he later died despite receiving emergency treatment.

Initial investigations into the shooting indicated that three masked individuals were involved in the attack and fled the scene. Witnesses told investigators that the attackers wore face coverings and dark clothing, while surveillance footage reportedly showed one of the suspects chasing the teenager before fleeing after the shooting. The death has raised concerns regarding possible bullying at Javits' school. His father, Thomas Frimpong, stated that his son had previously complained about being harassed by fellow students. According to Thomas Frimpong, two students had been involved in confrontations with Javits shortly before the shooting and were subsequently suspended from school. In response to the killing, U.S. civil rights lawyer Ben Crump announced he has been retained to represent the family of Javits Frimpong. Crump stated that Javits had moved from Ghana a year ago with the dream of becoming a doctor.

On November 10, 2026, Ghana's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, announced that he has spoken to Ben Crump about extending his services to other Ghanaians. cards.headline: Tthets’éhk’édélı̨ First Nation uses family-based council selection in Jean Marie River, N.W.T.

pages.text: The Tthets’éhk’édélı̨ First Nation in the Northwest Territories has spent nearly a decade using a unique leadership model in the Jean Marie River community. While the chief and two councillors representing youth and elders are elected, four other council seats are filled by representatives chosen by specific family groups. This system has generated differing perspectives on whether the approach fosters community unity or reinforces divisions between families. In 2025, 68 people lived in the community located on the banks of the Mackenzie River, approximately a two-hour drive from Fort Simpson.

In October, the community saw the election of a new chief, Paul Simon, along with new representatives for youth and elders. However, the four councillors joining them were selected through the family-based system rather than a general election. Under this arrangement, the three main families in the community—the Norwegian, Sanguez, and Hardisty families—each chose one representative. A fourth council seat is held by a representative from one of the three smallest families: the Sake, Gargan, or Minoza families.

Misty Ireland, a band member living 400 kilometres away in Hay River, recently completed a three-year term representing the Norwegian family. Ireland described being 'voluntold' to serve, noting that it is difficult to decline when a family requests participation. She expressed support for the family representative system, stating she believes it has helped bring band members into the political process who might otherwise have remained on the sidelines.

cards.headline: Farmers in Limpopo, South Africa use drumming and fire to deter elephants

pages.text: Smallholder farmers at Den Staat farm in South Africa’s Limpopo region are using creative methods to deter elephants from destroying crops that provide their income. As of November 10, 2026, more than 160 people live on the farm, where residents identify elephants as their most destructive concern. To protect their fields, farmers beat metal tins, hang empty white plastic containers on wires, and light fires to scare the animals away. Joeman Moyo, a farmer managing a 5-hectare (12.4-acre) plot, reported a conflict with an elephant in a tomato field where he used a torch and burned a tire to attempt to drive the animal away, though he noted the elephant returned once the fire died down.

Den Staat is part of the Greater Mapungubwe landscape, an area where elephants move across the borders of South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Botswana. While elephants are the primary concern for farmers, they are not the only animals raiding produce; farmers also lose crops to baboons, warthogs, zebras, and wildebeests. The land at Den Staat was returned to the Machete community in 2010 following historical forced removals under apartheid. cards.headline: Human rights advocates warn new FPIC guidelines in the Philippines threaten indigenous land rights

pages.text: Human rights advocates in the Philippines warn that revised guidelines for Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) raise serious concerns and threaten the land rights of indigenous peoples. The National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) updated the previous guidelines, which had been in place since 2012. FPIC is the process through which indigenous communities provide consent for projects proposed within their ancestral domains. Human rights lawyer Raymond Baguilat stated that the revised guidelines risk simplifying the process to facilitate business faster rather than ensuring that indigenous peoples' rights are fully respected.

A primary criticism of the new NCIP guidelines involves stricter time frames for community assemblies. Under the revised rules, assemblies must be completed within 10 days for large-scale projects with potential irreversible impacts. For projects with more limited impacts, the guidelines require the assembly to be completed within five days. Advocates also criticize how proposed projects are categorized based on their expected degree of impact on the land, arguing that this categorization appears to undervalue the impacts on people and land. The approval process for these projects varies depending on the category assigned.

cards.headline: 237-million-year-old fossils in China reveal armored sea-dwelling amphibian

pages.text: Two exceptionally well-preserved skeletons discovered in China's Guizhou Province reveal an ancient amphibian, *Gerrothorax maritimus*, that lived entirely in the ocean. This finding is notable because no amphibian known to be alive on November 11, 2026, is known to live its entire life in a marine environment. While mammals, reptiles, and birds include species that live entirely at sea without relying on land for food or fresh water, scientists had not previously identified convincing fossil evidence of an amphibian with this ability. Among more than 8,000 amphibian species living on November 11, 2026, fewer than 2% have any ability to tolerate salt, and none are known to spend their entire lives in marine environments. The fossils date back nearly 237 million years to the Late Triassic period, a time when the Guizhou region was submerged beneath an ancient ocean hundreds of miles from major landmasses. The unusual animal had a broad, flattened body protected by bony armor and was approximately the size of a giant salamander. Researchers believe *Gerrothorax maritimus* spent much of its life on the seafloor, waiting to ambush passing prey.

The discovery was made by an international team of researchers from the University of California, Davis, Peking University, and the Geological Museum of Guizhou. Their findings were published in *Nature Ecology & Evolution*. Ryosuke Motani, a professor in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at UC Davis and the study's corresponding author, stated that the team has been studying the ecosystem of this area to reconstruct it. Motani noted that while they have mostly been studying fish and marine reptiles from this location, this amphibian represents a very unusual member of the lineage.

cards.headline: Bennu asteroid analysis suggests amino acids may have originated in different parts of the solar system

pages.text: Analysis of amino acids from the Bennu asteroid and the Murchison meteorite suggests that these molecules, which are the building blocks of proteins necessary for life, may have formed through the same process but originated in different locations within the solar system. Researchers found that the carbon and nitrogen atoms within these molecules likely came from different reservoirs, according to a study published in Communications Earth & Environment. This finding provides a potential link between space chemistry and the origins of life on Earth by tracing the history of the atoms that compose these essential organic compounds.

To reach these conclusions, a research team including scientists from Penn State used a technique to study isotopes, which are slight variations in the mass of an atom within a molecular compound. Because isotope ratios act as a measurable tag, they can link specific molecules to the chemical processes or reservoirs where they were formed. By measuring these isotopes, the team could identify clues regarding the older history of specific atoms within the amino acids. The study utilized unique isotope instruments, including one located only at Penn State, to examine samples from the Bennu asteroid—delivered in 2023 by NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission—and the Murchison meteorite, which fell to Earth in 1969.

The researchers reported that the wide range of isotope values measured in both the Bennu and Murchison samples was surprising. This variation suggests that the carbon and nitrogen atoms within the amino acids did not originate from a single source. Lead author Ophélie Mcintosh, a former postdoctoral researcher in Penn State's Department of Geosciences, noted that while most studies focus on the quantity and distribution of amino acids, their research focused on how they are formed. The Bennu sample provided specific insight because it was delivered directly from space without terrestrial contamination.

cards.headline: Ancient viral DNA discovered in 1,000-year-old European manuscripts

pages.text: An international research team led by University College Dublin (UCD) has discovered ancient viral DNA preserved in the animal skins used to create parchment for medieval manuscripts. By analyzing these historical documents, researchers uncovered the first genetic evidence that sheeppox virus (SPPV) was spreading through European sheep flocks long before modern times. This discovery, published in Science Advances, allows scientists to reconstruct more than 3,500 years of the virus's evolution. The findings reveal that manuscripts preserved for their cultural significance can also serve as sources of valuable biological evidence because parchment was traditionally produced using prepared animal hides from sheep, goats, and cattle.

The researchers identified viral DNA in several historically significant documents, including the 1,000-year-old York Gospels, which is considered one of the finest surviving illuminated manuscripts from the early Anglo-Saxon period. The study also examined the Corpus Glossary at Corpus Christi College Cambridge, one of the earliest English dictionaries, alongside other medieval manuscripts from Britain and continental Europe. Sheeppox is a highly contagious disease that can spread through flocks with alarming speed. It can kill large numbers of infected animals, particularly young sheep, and causes major economic losses by reducing meat, milk, and wool production.

cards.headline: Gravitational waves could reveal new exoplanets, according to NASA-led studies

pages.text: Two studies led by NASA astrophysicists suggest the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) observatory could detect a unique population of exoplanets—worlds outside our solar system—by observing gravitational waves. These waves are tiny ripples in space-time caused by orbiting masses. The findings, published in The Astrophysical Journal, detail how LISA could identify planets orbiting double white dwarf systems, which are binary pairs of white dwarfs in tight orbits. While the possibility of detecting exoplanets around these systems was first proposed by Japanese astronomer Naoki Seto in 2008, these new studies provide more detail on the detection method and potential confirmation processes.

The first study, authored by Casey McGrath, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, and NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, examines the detection method. McGrath determined the specific planet masses and orbital periods where this method would work most effectively. The detection process is similar to radial velocity, a method that uses light to find exoplanets around nearby stars. In the case of LISA, an exoplanet's presence would become imprinted on the gravitational wave signal produced by the orbiting white dwarfs. A second paper, by McGrath and co-authors, investigates how these planets could be confirmed using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope.

LISA is a mission led by the European Space Agency (ESA) that is currently in development and slated for launch in the mid-2030s. NASA is a collaborative partner in the mission, contributing telescopes, critical hardware, and engineering and scientific support. The observatory is designed to detect gravitational waves to help scientists better understand the universe.

cards.headline: Cambodia’s mangrove forests provide refuge for threatened wildlife, study finds

pages.text: A seven-year study conducted by the Phnom Penh-based private company Fishing Cat Ecological Enterprise (FCEE) found that Cambodia’s mangrove forests and associated wetlands serve as critical refuge for several threatened and elusive species. Researchers deployed camera traps across 156 coastal and riverine mangrove sites within the Peam Krasop Wildlife Sanctuary and the adjacent Koh Kapik Ramsar site between 2017 and 2023. These two areas together form Cambodia’s largest mangrove expanse. While the research team initially focused on the fishing cat, they expanded their scope to include other mammal species to support broader conservation efforts, according to FCEE director and study corresponding author Vanessa Herranz Muñoz.

Camera footage from the study identified several threatened species utilizing the habitat. These included fishing cats (Prionailurus viverrinus) in mangrove thickets, smooth-coated otters (Lutra perspicillata) in fringe river channels, leopard cats (Prionailurus bengalensis) and hairy-nosed otters (Lutra sumatrana) near rivers, and large-spotted civets (Viverra megaspila) in swamp forests dominated by paperbark trees (Melaleuca spp.). Despite the presence of these animals, researchers observed that four threatened species declined over the seven-year study period: the endangered long-tailed macaque (Macaca fascicularis), the endangered large-spotted civet, and the vulnerable fishing cat and smooth-coated otter. The adaptable common palm civet (Paradoxurus hermaphroditus) was the only species to show signs of increase. The critically endangered Sunda pangolin (Manis javanica) and the endangered hairy-nosed otter remained difficult to detect.

Vanessa Herranz Muñoz noted that conservation efforts must extend beyond mangrove forests to include surrounding ecosystems. She stated that protecting Melaleuca forests is essential for the endangered large-spotted civet, while riverine mixed mangroves are critical for the hairy-nosed otter, which is considered the rarest otter in the world. A 2023 biodiversity survey conducted by the conservation NGO Fauna & Flora and the FCEE, which also involved Herranz Muñoz, identified more than 700 unique species within the Peam Krasop and Koh Kapik areas.

cards.headline: Coyote populations persist on North Carolina's Outer Banks despite removal efforts

pages.text: Coyote populations on the Outer Banks of North Carolina appear to be a permanent fixture, persisting despite long-term lethal removal programs intended to protect shore-nesting birds and sea turtles. A study by North Carolina State University researchers found that between 45 and 60 coyotes inhabit the islands at any one time, even as the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service work to manage their impact on local wildlife nesting habitats. Over the course of the study, researchers identified 62 individual coyotes through DNA analysis of fecal samples collected across seven islands: Bodie, Pea, Hatteras, Ocracoke, North Core, South Core, and Shackleford Banks. This research represents the first peer-reviewed study to estimate coyote density and population size on any barrier island.

The study, conducted over three seasons between 2024 and 2025, suggests that removal efforts face significant challenges due to population turnover. In 2024, the National Park Service removed 14 coyotes from Bodie and Hatteras islands, yet researchers continued to detect coyotes on both islands throughout the year as new individuals replaced those that were removed. Lead author Daniel Sossover, a research associate in the Department of Forestry and Environmental Resources at NC State University and at the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences, noted that the National Park Service has spent significant funds for more than a decade attempting to manage the coyotes through lethal removal. Sossover stated that the findings suggest a need to recognize coyotes as part of the ecosystem and find ways to coexist with them. The study's collaborators included NC State University professors Roland Kays and Liz Kierepka, and Nathan Hostetter of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

Coyotes have moved into the Outer Banks over the last two decades, likely by swimming between islands or crossing bridges. This expansion has caused ecological and management concerns for residents, visitors, and wildlife managers. From 2009 to 2025, the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service lethally removed more than 170 coyotes from Cape Hatteras National Seashore, Cape Lookout National Seashore, and Pea Island National Wildlife Refuge. Sossover indicated that removal often fails because coyote populations may respond to heavy removal pressure by breeding earlier, producing larger litter sizes, or moving into removal areas, allowing local populations to bounce back rapidly.

cards.headline: Researchers identify geological sources of blue azurite used by Ancestral Pueblo communities

pages.text: A research team led by Kari Schleher of the University of New Mexico has identified the geological sources of azurite used by Ancestral Pueblo communities approximately 1,400 years ago. Azurite is a copper mineral with a vivid blue color that was used as a pigment or paint. The study, according to a statement from the University of New Mexico, focused on 12 azurite specimens recovered in the Four Corners region of the American Southwest. By analyzing the isotopes of lead, strontium, and copper in these specimens, scientists were able to trace the material back to specific locations. Most of the analyzed samples were found to have been collected in the Lisbon Valley, while two samples originated from the Zuni Mountains in New Mexico.

To determine the origins of the pigment, the scientists first analyzed two samples of azurite from known mining sites in New Mexico and Utah used by Ancestral Pueblo people. This provided a baseline for comparing the 12 specimens found in the Four Corners region. Future research by the team will include analyzing more azurite samples held at the New Mexico Mining Museum. Schleher also stated that the team plans to consult local oral histories regarding traditional territories and the use of mines.
